title: Irn Burnout
excerpt: Exploring Scottish artists while recovering from burnout
body:
In 2025, I finally realised I was burned out. It wasn’t sudden; it wasn’t one particular event or challenge at work. It was 15 years of not having proper techniques to deal with life’s challenges.

I took time off work, I got into therapy, and I began processing and healing from a particularly eventful few years. At the end of the year, on Hogmanay, I sat down with my best friend and made a bingo card of goals for 2026, all umbrella’d under the theme “Connection”, artfully doodled on a sheet of paper and stuck up on my wall. In the following months, I barely travelled back to Scotland; I wanted to stay put, recover, and connect to the place I now call home. Although, in a way, I kinda have two homes.

My Scottish hometown of 12,000 people is the kind of place where you always bump into someone you know, everything is walkable, lots of nature, one high school, and no escape. So when I finished school, I moved to Edinburgh, but after five years I still wanted more; I ventured across the pond and docked in the Netherlands.

Now, after a burnout and a decade as an expat (read immigrant), I find myself seeking out the Scottish experience through gigs. When a Scottish band or artist comes to town, I want to go, to connect, and to support Scottish artists. So without further ado, here is my rundown of the Scottish artists I’ve seen in the Netherlands this year.

Biffy Clyro - The Futique Tour

Kicking it off with a bang, I saw Biffy Clyro’s The Futique Tour in January. As a Scot, you can’t beat the feeling of being in a crowd filled with fans chanting “Mon the Biff!”. Three decades after forming in Kilmarnock, they still maintain that humble small-town local band feel, but it's combined with the crowds and huge fan base of a “best band in the world”. I’ve been a fan since I was a teenager; sung their songs at karaoke, listened to their albums on repeat, but this was my first time seeing them live.

January was a difficult time for me personally; the winter and burnout blues were hitting hard. But it was also reflective; I spent days lost in thought, looking back on the past and forward to the future. Not unlike Biffy’s latest album Futique, an amalgamation of Future and Antique. I attended the gig solo, something that I’ve gotten pretty comfortable doing in recent years. I can definitely recommend it; you’re never truly alone when you’re surrounded by people who are there for the same reason as you. I particularly resonated with A Little Love, a song about love and connection between friends, and A Thousand and One, a love letter to growth and owning past mistakes.

The gig itself was typical Biffy. Shirtless, tattooed Simon Neil, his characteristic Scottish-accented voice, powerful strobing lights, and stark yet commanding staging, red velvet risers mirroring the album art. The only difference was that James Johnston, on bass, was missing. Shortly before touring, they announced his temporary absence while he focuses on his mental health. It struck a chord at a time when I was learning to do the same.

Seen at AFAS, Amsterdam, 30th January 2026

Belle and Sebastian - If You’re Feeling Sinister

Belle and Sebastian are an indie pop band formed in the city of Glasgow in 1994. Their two gigs at Paradiso were part of their 30th anniversary tour, two separate nights featuring Tigermilk (1996) and If You’re Feeling Sinister (1996) respectively. You rarely get to hear an album played in full and in order at a concert. To me, it feels like hearing it the way it was intended, allowing you to fully connect to the experience.

We had a great view from the balcony, and the atmosphere was infectious. You could see Stuart Murdoch having a great time on stage, and that energy quickly transferred to the crowd, who were bopping along to all their hits. Murdoch's filmmaking side appeared in the projections on the three white drapes behind the stage, setting the atmosphere throughout. On stage, the band not only had the classic indie pop instruments but also strings and synth, a full chamber pop extravaganza.

After the album run-through, they also performed a second half made up of classics from their other albums, ending with The Boy with the Arab Strap, during which all the VIP ticket holders were invited up on stage to dance with the band. That’s Belle and Sebastian for you; pure, uncomplicated Scottish joy.

I went to this one with friends. Over the last few years, my burnout crept up on me. In hindsight, one warning sign that I ignored was that I wasn’t open to connecting with new people. Despite this, Susy found a way in anyway. Meeting as co-bridesmaids at a hen-do, we immediately understood each other, bonding over being the nerds in a group and a shared talent for noticing the peculiarities. When we realised we both lived in the Netherlands, “we should get coffee” turned into something real. And we discovered that, together with her husband Louis, we have quite similar music tastes. I’ve since watched her build a life with Louis, an amazing father who packed up their entire home while she was heavily pregnant and didn't utter a single complaint. These are the friends who pulled me out of my own head when I'd stopped letting people in, and brought me to this gig.

Seen at Paradiso, Amsterdam, 3rd March 2026

Daniel Sloss - Bitter

Daniel Sloss failed to disappoint once again. Seeing him live is one of those things I always do; it’s life sustenance. Taylor and I have seen every one of his shows since he was just a young lad doing small venues at the fringe (excluding that unmentionable time in 2020). This time, we bought tickets almost a year in advance; her visit to Amsterdam planned around Sloss. This was his 13th show, titled Bitter, and it was just as unapologetic, brutally honest, and hilarious as ever.

It’s a show about politics, abusive power dynamics, and knowing who you are - surprise, surprise, that resonated with me. The standout bit of his show was the section about Russell Brand. Channel 4 asked Sloss, alongside many other comedians, to comment on the situation in the comedy scene regarding Brand. He shares the internal battle he faced, unsure whether speaking against Brand would harm his career. He decided he couldn’t be a silent bystander, and hoped others would do the same. He was the only comedian who went on record.

Speaking out brought him a lot of backlash: death threats, industry alienation, and quiet resentment within the circuit. But he still stands headstrong.

Sloss articulates that speaking up about rumours already known within the comedy circuit should be the bare minimum. Yet, many people in the industry, especially senior agents/execs, keep quiet. And by doing so, they became complicit in Brand’s abuse. He argues that this silence has allowed Brand to maintain a massive career despite the open secrets.

I am familiar with situations that bear some resemblance to what Sloss describes: An abusive power dynamic, people in positions of authority who stayed silent, and apologies that came too late. I have also watched someone continue working when they shouldn’t have. So, as a long-term fan of Sloss, I have never felt prouder. It’s truly admirable when a person stands up for what they believe in despite the negative consequences. Even better when that person is just a small-town Scottish lad.

Seen at Koninklijk Theatre Carré, Amsterdam, 7th March 2026

Wet Wet Wet - Love Is All Around Europe

This adventure was a bit of a disappointment. Wet Wet Wet is a band formed in 1982 in the Scottish town of Clydebank. They are best known for their cover of Love Is All Around, which was featured in Four Weddings and a Funeral. Not to be confused with When You Say Nothing At All, featured in Notting Hill, a mistake not one but two people made when I said I was going. Both films are 90s romcoms written by Richard Curtis and starring Hugh Grant.

So what put me off? The band has a new frontman. A younger guy who was too polished and sounded like a tribute band singer, overproduced, autotuned, and entirely lacking the soul of Marti Pellow’s voice. It made the whole show feel like an over-glamourised cruise-ship moment. The OGs seemed to be aware of this, too, as they tried a little too hard to oversell Kevin Simm. I have since found out he was a member of Liberty X (from Popstars) and also won The Voice in 2016, so boyband karaoke is literally in his DNA. It was still a fun evening; they sang all the classics, but it wasn’t the vibe I was looking for. Not every attempt to connect to your roots delivers what you hoped for, but if you don’t take risks, you won’t discover the gems.

Seen at Paradiso, Amsterdam, 4th May 2026

Eric Clapton

Ok, I know, I know, he’s not Scottish. But newsflash: neither am I, fully. Technically, I’m 50% English. So here we are.

My evening at Clapton’s gig was one of those beautifully spontaneous moments that never would have happened if I wasn’t beating burnout. I didn't have a plan. I knew about the concert but wasn't sure I'd have the energy after swimming. Then I came out of the pool, felt the sun on my face, and had a sudden burst of yes energy.

I biked to Noorderpark, hopped on the metro, and nervously checked Ticketswap the whole way to Bijlmer, still not entirely sure if I would end up at Clapton or Paul Simon. I bought a ticket whilst being herded along with the crowd from the metro to Ziggo Dome.

It wasn't a cheap evening, but Clapton maintains his legendary status for a reason, and he did not disappoint. His pared-down show was epic: just him, jamming with his band, weaving covers, originals, and riffs that gave me chills. There’s always a worry seeing artists later in their careers, but Clapton did not sound his age; he still has it. I had a friend there too, and though we sat apart, we rode home together and dissected the whole thing.

It's this curiosity for the novel that made me leave Scotland in the first place, always looking, always exploring, and this evening made me feel like I was finally discovering this side of myself after burnout had hidden it for a long time. Sometimes the best adventures, the ones that make you feel most alive, come when you leap.

Seen at Ziggo Dome, Amsterdam, 24th April 2026

Concerts have always brought me joy, and I’ve always left them feeling on top of the world. Now, in my 30s and healing from burnout, I finally have the money, the energy, and the self-confidence to do what I want when I want and prioritise these experiences.

The bingo card is still up on my wall. “Go to 5 gigs” was one square, but I had no idea they’d all end up being British gigs. Maybe that’s the beauty of having two homes, not choosing between them but finding one inside the other. One gig at a time. I will say, hearing all the Scottish accents on stages 500 miles (close enough) from my home hits like a freshly cracked can of Irn-Bru every time. Here’s to chasing life with open arms.
